Kenji Tanaka — Stair-Climbing Locomotion said about it: (E49, physicsforums.com — Disc brake effectiveness varies on rotor size?) that braking torque equals retarding friction force times contact radius, and I take from US20090133517A1 - Mechanical Tri-Wheel Retention Assembly for Stair-Climbing Wheeled Vehicle - Google Patents (E44, patents.google.com — US20090133517A1 - Mechanical Tri-Wheel Retention Assembly for Stair-Climbing Wheeled Vehicle - Google Patents) that the clutch can act as a brake to lock the truck to the stairs if the user stops on ascent or descent.
Elena Ruiz — Human Factors & Single-Operator Safety said about it: As Elena Ruiz, single-operator safety: The hold must not live in the hands, so I confirm what Kenji Tanaka takes from The Bicycle Physics of the Hydraulic Brake (E45, The Bicycle Physics of the Hydraulic Brake) that clamp times radius makes torque and from US20090133517A1 - Mechanical Tri-Wheel Retention Assembly for Stair-Climbing Wheeled Vehicle - Google Patents (E44, US20090133517A1 - Mechanical Tri-Wheel Retention Assembly for Stair-Climbing Wheeled Vehicle - Google Patents) that a lock can hold the truck on stairs if the user stops, because that is the dead-man brake lever on both grips (C7) plus tooth park hold in the disc sketch (E52).
Tomas Lind — Folding & Van Integration said about it: I take from the US20090133517A1 - Mechanical Tri-Wheel Retention Assembly for Stair-Climbing Wheeled Vehicle - Google Patents (E44) that a separate clutch locks the cluster on stairs, and I take from the Load securing for lashing cargo - good quality and strength (E60) that under European Norm (EN) 12195-1 restraint must hold 0.8 times forward weight and 0.5 times to rear and side.
